overview: Roofers install, repair and replace roofs on homes and commercial buildings. They inspect damage, estimate materials and labor, and work with shingles, metal, tar and waterproofing. O*NET rates knowledge of building and construction at 4.7 out of 5 for this job and mechanical knowledge at 4.01. Most roofers learn on the job, often starting as helpers, and a high school diploma is typical. The BLS May 2025 median is $55,440 across 135,490 jobs. The work is outdoors in all weather, at height and on your feet, with tight deadlines when storms hit.
pay: Roofers earn a median of $55,440, and the top 10% earn $81,720 or more. Illinois has the highest state median at $77,900, 41% above the national figure, followed by New Jersey and Minnesota. Florida has the most roofers, 23,550, with a median of $47,590, and California has 21,190.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $55,440 a year. The lowest 10% earn under $37,460, usually new helpers, and the top 10% earn $81,720 or more. Illinois, New Jersey and Minnesota pay the most, while Mississippi ($44,940) and Oklahoma ($43,680) have the lowest state medians.

faq.q: How do you become a roofer?
faq.a: Most roofers start as helpers and learn on the job over 1 to 2 years. O*NET places the job in Job Zone 2, which usually means a high school diploma. Some join a union apprenticeship, which mixes paid work with classroom training and can lead to higher wages.

Yes. In O*NET data, roofers rank above 95% of U.S. jobs for tight deadlines and for time spent on their feet. The work is outdoors in all weather and at height, so safety training and fall protection are essential. Cautiousness and dependability stand out as work styles.

faq.q: What other jobs can roofers do?
faq.a: Close matches include masonry helpers (84%), surface mining machine operators (75%) and metal layout workers (73%), based on O*NET 31.0. Layout Workers earn $63,870, 15% more than roofers, according to BLS May 2025, and work indoors in manufacturing.
